overview: The House of Savoy governed a changing collection of Alpine and Italian territories, with Turin becoming its capital in 1563. Its rulers acquired the Sardinian crown in 1720. The three map labels belong to successive phases of this dynastic state, although “Sardinia-Piedmont” is premature for the map’s 1650 starting date.

periods.title: Duchy and Alpine state
periods.summary: French occupation interrupted rule; restoration in 1559 preceded the transfer of the capital to Turin.

periods.title: A Sardinian kingdom with mainland territories
periods.summary: The Sardinian crown joined a state whose court and major administrative center remained on the mainland.

periods.title: French disruption and island monarchy
periods.summary: French domination displaced mainland Savoyard government before restoration in 1815.

periods.title: Restoration, constitution and Italian unification
periods.summary: The restored kingdom adopted a constitution in 1848 and became the institutional core of the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

sections.title: A capital powered by water and work

items.text: When Marguerite of France formally entered Turin on 7 February 1563, municipal officials arranged a canopy and prepared the streets. City accounts record the work and expense behind the ceremony. A royal welcome required ordinary people to build, organize and pay, not simply wave at a procession.

Turin’s municipal mills used water from the Dora to grind grain. In 1679 the city expanded their capacity as population and demand grew. Bread depended on machinery, water management and decisions about shared infrastructure as well as on farmers’ harvests.

Silk production connected mulberry growing and silkworm keeping with skilled processing. In the 1660s Turin supported a water-powered silk mill associated with Galleani. The technology improved production, but luxurious cloth still depended on the labor of people far removed from the court wearing it.

A silk works commissioned at Venaria in 1670 included machinery and a professional training school. Visitors could see the work from the street. Industrial skill was something to teach and display: this royal neighborhood offered a glimpse of manufacturing as well as grand architecture.

Before mechanization, silk thread was largely processed by hand, with women providing much of that labor. The machines produced a finer, stronger and more consistent thread. The change affected working routines as well as the appearance and value of the finished material.

In Sardinia, eighteenth-century reforms changed the language of schools and official business from Spanish to Italian. The universities at Cagliari and Sassari reopened in 1764 and 1765. These were major institutional changes, not evidence that every island household immediately changed its everyday language.

The 1820 enclosure edict encouraged private landholding, but access to land was already woven into pastoral and village life. Closing land could disrupt shared grazing and other uses. Property reform brought conflict as well as promises of agricultural improvement.

The 1847 administrative fusion applied mainland institutions to Sardinia. An island already sharing a monarch with the mainland had retained distinct arrangements. A shared crown and a single administrative system were therefore different things, with practical consequences for how people were governed.

In 1832 Giuseppe Cottolengo began a new charitable institution at Valdocco in a modest building with a stable, hayloft and an upstairs room. It welcomed poor sick people who could be excluded by other hospitals. The hospital complex grew from these very ordinary premises.

Turin’s wells and fountains could supply too little water, and some water was polluted. A new distribution network brought water from the Val Sangone. Its 1859 inauguration activated the fountain in Piazza Carlo Felice, making an engineering project visible in a familiar public space.

Charles Albert granted the Statuto in 1848 after pressure for constitutional reform. It established a framework with a king and two parliamentary chambers. The document changed government, but the monarch still appointed the Senate; constitutional government did not mean everyone could vote.

Article 24 reads “Tutti i regnicoli, qualunque sia il loro titolo o grado, sono eguali dinanzi alla legge.” It means “All subjects of the kingdom, whatever their title or rank, are equal before the law.” The Italian legal text states a principle; it does not prove equal political participation.

ending.text: In 1861 the monarchy became the Kingdom of Italy, with the Savoy dynasty continuing on its throne. This was a transformation into a larger state, not the disappearance of its people or institutions. The map’s 1878 endpoint should not be read as the end of an independent Sardinian kingdom.
